companies.name: ArmaturaSec d.o.o.
companies.about:
ArmaturaSec d.o.o. has been building network security hardware in Zrenjanin since 2008. We started by selling simple firewall appliances to regional electricity distributors who needed to segment their control networks from corporate IT. Over fifteen years that focus narrowed: today every product we ship is designed specifically for operational technology environments — the kind of networks that run pumps, switchgear, and assembly lines, not office computers.

Our customers are energy utilities, water treatment operators, and discrete manufacturers in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. They are not looking for cloud dashboards or vendor lock-in; they need a device that sits in a metal cabinet at a substation or pump station, runs for years without attention, and tells someone when something is wrong.

We have 67 people in Zrenjanin. About half write firmware or do hardware bring-up; the rest handle sales, installation, and support. Our head of engineering, Radovan Čičić, joined from a SCADA integrator in 2011 and has led every product generation since. We do not resell other vendors' software. Everything that runs on our appliances — the protocol parsers, the access control engine, the alerting logic — is written and maintained by our own team.

NetGuard-OT Mini: DIN-rail form factor variant for smaller substations and pump stations

challenges.text: We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.
challenges.detail: Our ProtoSense module watches Modbus and BACnet traffic and is supposed to flag anything that looks wrong. The problem is that none of our clients has ever given us a packet capture that contains a confirmed attack. A few of them have been running their networks for twenty years with no security monitoring at all, so if they were compromised they would not know. We have plenty of normal traffic — we have collected several terabytes of captures from consenting clients over the past three years — but we have nothing labelled as malicious. We tried building a supervised classifier once, fed it data from public ICS datasets, and it flagged so many false positives in real deployments that clients started switching the alerts off. What we actually need is something that learns what normal looks like on a specific site and raises a flag when behaviour drifts from that baseline. We have the traffic archives, we have the hardware to run inference on-device, and we have one engineer who has been reading about anomaly detection for six months. We need a method that works with no attack examples and that we can explain to a plant manager in plain language.

challenges.text: Our appliance firmware update process currently requires a technician on-site at the customer's substation; we want secure over-the-air updates, but every approach we've prototyped either has an unacceptable attack surface or fails when the GPRS link drops mid-transfer.
challenges.detail: Every time we release a firmware update we have to send someone to the customer site to plug in a USB drive. For a substation forty kilometres outside Novi Sad that is manageable. For a client in a mountain valley in Bosnia it means a full day of travel. We want to push updates over the cellular link the appliance already uses for remote monitoring. We have prototyped three approaches. The first used a plain HTTPS pull with a signature check; a security review inside the team found the key storage on the current hardware was not good enough and an attacker with physical access could extract the signing key. The second used a dual-partition scheme with rollback; it worked fine on a stable connection but when the GPRS link dropped mid-transfer the bootloader left the device in a state we could not recover remotely, which is unacceptable at an unmanned site. The third prototype added a download manager with resume support but the code size pushed us over the flash budget on our older hardware variant. We need a design that tolerates interrupted transfers, does not require hardware we cannot retrofit, and does not introduce a new remote code execution path. We have a draft threat model document we can share.

challenges.text: Three clients in Serbia and one in Bosnia asked us to provide a risk quantification report in euros — how much financial loss a specific vulnerability exposes them to — and we have no methodology for that; it's becoming a dealbreaker in contract negotiations.
challenges.detail: Four clients — three in Serbia and one in Bosnia — have asked us to attach a euro figure to each finding in our SecAudit reports. They want to be able to tell their board: this vulnerability could cost us this much. We understand why they ask. They need to justify remediation budgets. The problem is we have never done this and we are not sure our current data supports it. We have records of what the vulnerabilities were, we know roughly what downtime costs for a water utility or an electricity distributor, and we can find published incident cost studies from Western Europe. What we do not have is a repeatable calculation method that holds up when a procurement officer asks how we arrived at the number. We have looked at two published frameworks and found them either too abstract or built for IT environments where data breach costs dominate. Our clients care about production downtime, regulatory fines under Serbian energy law, and emergency response costs. We need a methodology we can apply consistently across different client types, document in a way that survives scrutiny, and run with our existing audit team without hiring a financial analyst.

challenges.text: Our quality assurance team writes regression tests by hand for every firmware release; with four hardware variants and monthly release cycles that's eating about 35% of total engineering time and we're still shipping bugs that automated tests should catch.
challenges.detail: We release firmware roughly once a month across four hardware variants: the original NetGuard-OT board, the Mini, and two older boards we still maintain for clients under long-term support contracts. Before each release our QA team runs a regression suite that they have been building by hand since 2015. The suite now has around 1,400 test cases. Writing new cases for a feature, updating old ones when hardware behaviour changes, and running everything on four boards takes about two and a half weeks of engineering time per cycle. That is the 35% figure. We have also shipped three bugs in the past year that the regression suite should have caught but did not because the relevant test cases were out of date. We have tried generating tests from our internal protocol specifications but the tooling we built for that was brittle and the team abandoned it. We want to get to a point where adding a feature automatically produces a skeleton of tests that a junior engineer can complete in an hour rather than a day. We are open to any approach that fits inside our existing Python-based test runner and does not require us to replace the hardware bench we already have.

companies.plans: ArmaturaSec intends to release a fifth hardware variant in late 2025 with a dedicated security processor to support on-device anomaly detection without affecting packet forwarding latency. We are also evaluating whether to open a small office in Sarajevo to reduce travel time for Bosnian client support.
companies.rd_capacity: We can dedicate one to two engineers part-time to a collaborative project, with access to our traffic archives, our hardware bench, and our existing firmware codebase under NDA.
companies.past_collaborations: We ran a one-semester student project with a technical faculty in Novi Sad in 2021 that produced a prototype BACnet fuzzer; the code was useful but the collaboration was not continued formally.

companies.name: Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o.
companies.about:
Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o. was founded in 2019 by siblings Miroslav and Tatjana Kovačević, who grew up in Zrenjanin and wanted to build something useful for the region's schools rather than chase the international mobile market. We make browser-based educational games for primary school children in Serbia and Hungary, sold mainly to municipalities, school boards, and NGOs that work in bilingual Serbian–Hungarian communities in Vojvodina.

Our games run in any modern browser without installation, which matters in schools where IT budgets are tight and devices are old. Subjects covered include mathematics, Serbian language, Hungarian language, and basic natural sciences for ages six to twelve.

We are a team of eight: two developers, one graphic designer, one illustrator, one sound designer, one pedagogy consultant, and two people handling sales, contracts, and support. Tatjana leads product and pedagogy; Miroslav leads development. Most of us have known each other since secondary school or university in Novi Sad.

Our customers include the City of Zrenjanin education office, three NGOs operating across Vojvodina, and two municipal education departments in southern Hungary. We work on fixed-price B2B contracts, usually tied to a school year, and we spend real time talking to teachers before we build anything.

challenges.text: Teachers tell us our math games are fun but they can't see whether a child is actually learning — we have clickstream data for 4,200 students but no way to tell if a pupil is guessing randomly versus genuinely understanding the material.
challenges.detail: Every time a child clicks an answer in our math games, we log it — timestamp, question ID, answer chosen, how long they took, how many attempts. We have that data for about 4,200 students across the 2022–23 and 2023–24 school years. The problem is we have no way to read anything meaningful out of it. A teacher told us last spring that one of her students had a 91% score but she was convinced the child understood nothing and was just clicking fast until something turned green. She was right — when she tested the child on paper the results were very different. We know this is a real problem but we do not know how to separate genuine learning from lucky guessing using the data we already have. We have exported the logs to CSV and tried building simple accuracy thresholds ourselves, but that does not catch the fast random clicker. We cannot afford to buy an off-the-shelf analytics platform, and we would not trust one that does not explain what it is doing. A good outcome for us would be a method or a small working tool that flags students who are likely guessing, so teachers can act on it. We would ideally have something testable before the 2025–26 school year starts.

challenges.text: We want to make our games accessible to children with dyslexia — about 12% of our user base based on teacher reports — but we don't know which font choices, colour contrasts, and text-presentation speeds actually help versus what is just marketing.
challenges.detail: About twelve percent of our users have been flagged by their teachers as having dyslexia or suspected reading difficulties. That is based on informal teacher reports, not formal diagnosis, so the real number could be different. Right now we use one standard font across all our games — a rounded sans-serif we picked because it looked friendly — and we set line spacing and reading speeds based on what felt reasonable to us. We have read about OpenDyslexic and similar fonts, and we have seen marketing material from several dyslexia-support tool companies claiming specific font and colour combinations help, but we cannot find solid evidence behind most of those claims that was actually tested with children in a classroom setting rather than adults in a lab. We tried switching one game to a higher-contrast colour scheme after a parent complained and got no useful feedback either way. We do not have the expertise to design a proper test ourselves, and we do not want to run experiments on children without knowing what we are doing. A good outcome would be a clear, evidence-backed set of recommendations for font, contrast, and text presentation speed that we can apply across our whole catalogue in one update cycle.

challenges.text: We applied for an Innovation Fund Voucher six months ago and the application was returned twice for administrative corrections — we don't have the internal capacity to manage grant paperwork and it's pulling our lead developer away from product work for weeks at a time.
challenges.detail: We applied for an Innovation Fund Voucher for Small Enterprises in early 2024. The application came back twice — once because the project description was categorised under the wrong activity code, and once because a supporting financial document was formatted incorrectly. Both corrections were straightforward once we understood what was needed, but figuring that out took weeks of back-and-forth with the fund administrator, and it was Miroslav who handled it because no one else on the team could. That pulled him away from a game update we had promised to a municipal customer. We are a small company and none of us trained for grant administration. We do not have budget to hire a consultant for every application, and we are likely to apply for other public funding in 2025. What we actually need is either someone who can help us build a reusable internal process for these applications, or a partnership arrangement where a research or support institution co-applies with us and carries the administrative side, while we contribute the product development work.

companies.plans: We want to expand our catalogue to cover grades five and six by the end of 2026, and we are exploring a pilot with one Hungarian school district for a fully bilingual game set tied to their local curriculum. We are also considering moving from VPS hosting to a managed cloud setup to reduce maintenance load on Miroslav.
companies.rd_capacity: Miroslav Kovačević is available for roughly one day per week for research-related work, with Tatjana available for pedagogy input on a similar basis, but both are constrained by ongoing contract delivery.
companies.past_collaborations: We worked informally with a primary school teacher network in Zrenjanin — coordinated by a local NGO called Vojvodina Creative Schools — to gather playtesting feedback during the development of our first math module in 2020, but we have no formal research or university collaboration history.

companies.name: AutomVoj a.d.
companies.about: AutomVoj a.d. has been building conveyor and sorting automation systems from its base in Zrenjanin since 1983. What started as a small workshop supplying domestic food processing plants has grown into a team of 212 engineers, electricians, and technicians shipping systems to customers in Serbia, Hungary, Romania, Austria, Slovenia, Croatia, and Slovakia. Our core business is straightforward: we design, manufacture, and commission PLC-based conveyor lines and automated sorting equipment for food and beverage producers who need reliable throughput in demanding environments — cold stores, wet wash areas, high-dust packaging halls. We do not chase every sector; we know food and beverage and we do it well. Our fabrication shop, electrical assembly area, and in-house testing floor are all under one roof on our Zrenjanin site. Most of our project managers started as commissioning engineers, so they understand what a line stoppage costs a customer at three in the morning. We have long-term supply relationships with component makers in Germany and Italy and we carry enough spares stock to respond within 48 hours on any system we have installed. Roughly 60 percent of our revenue now comes from repeat customers or referrals.

challenges.text: Our conveyor frames crack at the weld joints after roughly 18 months of operation in chilled environments; we've replaced 14 assemblies under warranty this year and we can't reproduce the failure in our workshop because we test at room temperature.
challenges.detail: Our conveyor frames are welded from mild steel hollow section and painted for corrosion resistance before delivery. When these systems run in customer cold stores — typically operating between 2 °C and 6 °C — we are seeing weld joint cracking at the main crossmember-to-stringer connections after about 18 months of continuous use. This year alone we have replaced 14 complete frame assemblies under warranty, which is costing us in material, travel, and lost engineer time. The frustrating part is that we have tried to reproduce the failure in our workshop and cannot do it. We test frames under load at room temperature and they pass without any problem. Our suspicion is that the combination of thermal cycling, condensation, and the vibration load from loaded belts is doing something we are not seeing at ambient conditions. We have photos and measurements of the cracked joints from site visits, and we still have two of the failed sections in storage. We do not currently have the equipment or know-how to test at low temperatures under cyclic load. A good outcome would be understanding exactly what is causing the cracks so we can change our welding procedure, filler material, or joint design and stop the warranty replacements.

challenges.text: Our PLC programs for different customers are each a custom spaghetti of ladder logic; when we want to push a safety patch we have to touch 38 separate codebases and it takes three engineers two full weeks.
challenges.detail: Over the years we have written a separate PLC program for almost every customer installation. Each one started from a rough template and then grew as the customer asked for changes during commissioning and after. Today we have 38 active codebases across our installed base, all written in ladder logic in TIA Portal, and they have drifted apart to the point where a safety-related patch — for example, an emergency stop sequence change required by a new machinery directive interpretation — has to be found, adapted, and tested in every single one of them. The last time we did this it took three of our engineers two full weeks, and they still found two sites where the logic was different enough that the standard fix did not apply cleanly. We know the answer is some form of modular library or structured code reuse, but every time we try to start, the daily project load pulls the engineers away. We have one senior PLC programmer, Dragan Ilić, who understands the full picture, but he is also our lead on active commissioning projects. We need a practical approach that does not require us to rewrite everything at once and that our team can actually maintain going forward.

challenges.text: We need a €2 million investment to open a second assembly hall, and our bank wants a three-year cash-flow model with sensitivity analysis that our CFO doesn't have the capacity to prepare before the Q3 deadline.
challenges.detail: We have planning permission and a cleared site adjacent to our existing building for a second assembly hall, which would let us run two large projects in parallel and cut our delivery lead times significantly. The total investment is around €2 million covering the building shell, electrical infrastructure, and a new overhead crane. We have a bank that is willing to discuss the loan but their condition before they will issue a term sheet is a three-year cash-flow model with sensitivity analysis showing how the business performs under different revenue and cost scenarios. Our CFO, Milena Varga, manages day-to-day financial operations well, but building a robust forward-looking model of this kind is outside what she normally does, and she does not have the time to learn it from scratch before the bank's Q3 deadline, which falls at the end of September 2024. We have the historical financial data — five years of audited accounts, project margin records, and a pipeline of signed and probable orders. We need someone who can structure that data into a credible model and help Milena understand it well enough to present it and answer questions from the bank.

challenges.text: Noise from our servo drives is injecting harmonics back into client factory grids and we've had two complaints from clients whose measurement instruments were affected; we don't have the tools to characterise the emission spectrum properly.
challenges.detail: Two of our clients — a dairy processing plant and a packaged-goods warehouse — have complained in the past year that precision measurement instruments on their production floors are behaving erratically. Both sites use our conveyor systems with Siemens SINAMICS frequency drives on the main drive motors. Our internal investigation points to harmonic current emissions from the drives feeding back into the building's low-voltage grid and causing interference. We have added standard line reactors on both installations as a first step and the complaints have reduced but not stopped. The problem is that we do not have the test equipment to measure the actual emission spectrum on site — we cannot tell our clients what frequencies are being injected, at what levels, or how those compare to the applicable EN standards for harmonic disturbance. Without that data we are guessing at solutions. We would like to characterise the emission properly, understand which part of our drive configuration is most responsible, and arrive at a consistent design rule we can apply to new installations so this does not keep coming up. Budget for this is limited; we are looking for a practical engineering solution, not a research project.

companies.plans: AutomVoj intends to increase its export share to 55 percent of revenue within three years, targeting food logistics customers in Central Europe, and is evaluating an entry into automated poultry processing lines as a second vertical. The second assembly hall, once financed, is expected to be operational by mid-2026.
companies.rd_capacity: We have no dedicated R&D department; technical development happens informally through project work, led by our chief engineer and two senior automation engineers who allocate time between live projects and improvement work.
companies.past_collaborations: AutomVoj completed a one-year joint development project with Fakultet tehničkih nauka in Novi Sad in 2019 on drive energy monitoring, which resulted in an internal measurement tool but was not published or commercialised.

companies.sector: Insurtech — embedded micro-insurance and parametric products
companies.about:
OsiguroMi d.o.o. je insurtech kompanija iz Novog Sada, osnovana 2019. godine sa jednom idejom: da osiguranje prestane da bude papirologija i postane tihi servis ugrađen u alate koje ljudi već koriste. Umesto da korisnik kupuje polisu na posebnom sajtu, naša tehnologija se integriše direktno u aplikacije za rezervaciju putovanja, agro-platforme i prodajne sisteme organizatora festivala — i polisa nastaje u trenutku transakcije.

Radimo sa B2B partnerima širom Srbije i EU: putničkim platformama, zadrugama, organizatorima open-air događaja. Naš tim od 58 zaposlenih dolazi iz osiguranja, softverskog inženjerstva i analize podataka. Osnivači Milena Čabarkapa i Dragan Horvat prethodno su radili u reosiguranju i fintech sektoru, što je oblikovalo naš pristup: prvo model, pa produkt.

Ono što nas razlikuje nije marketing — razlikuje nas API koji se može uključiti za manje od jednog radnog dana i parametarski okidači koji ne zahtevaju korisnikov zahtev za naknadu. Isplata se dešava automatski ili ne, na osnovu merljivih podataka: kašnjenje leta, količina padavina, otkazivanje događaja. Nema formulara, nema čekanja. Klijenti naših partnera to retko primete dok im ne zatreba, a onda primete odmah.

challenges.text: Our weather-triggered crop parametric product pays out when measured rainfall at the nearest official station drops below a threshold, but farmers tell us the station is sometimes 30 km away and their field got rain while the station recorded drought — we're paying out when we shouldn't and refusing when we should.
challenges.detail: Naš agro-proizvod isplaćuje naknadu kada zvanična meteorološka stanica zabeleži količinu padavina ispod ugovorenog praga u određenom periodu. Problem je što najbliža stanica nekad stoji 30 kilometara od parcele — a na tih 30 km može biti planinski venac, rečna dolina ili urbana zona, sve to menja lokalne padavine drastično. Dobijamo povratne informacije od partnera u Vojvodini i Bačkoj da su im isplate stizale kad polje nije ni presušilo, ili da ih nije bilo kad su urod izgubili. Pokušali smo da korigujemo prag na osnovu istorijskih razlika između stanica i terena, ali to je gruba aproksimacija. Imamo pristup RHMZS podacima i podacima tri privatne agrometeo mreže, ukupno oko 140 tačaka merenja u regionu. Razmišljali smo o satelitskim indeksima vlažnosti tla, ali nismo sigurni kako pouzdano spojiti te izvore u jedan okidač. Cilj je da do sledeće sezone ispravljamo isplate na osnovu prostorno tačnijih procena padavina po parceli, bez potpune zamene ugovornog praga.

challenges.text: We process around 9,000 travel-delay claims per month fully automatically, but our internal audit found that 3.1% of payouts were triggered by data errors from the flight-status API rather than genuine delays — that's real money leaking out every month.
challenges.detail: Mesečno obrađujemo oko 9.000 zahteva za naknadu zbog kašnjenja leta, potpuno automatski, bez ljudskog uvida. Interna revizija za treće tromesečje 2023. pokazala je da je 3,1% isplata aktivirano greškama u podacima dobavljača statusa letova — pogrešni vremenski žigovi, dupli unosi, letovi koji su tehnički otkazani ali su prikazani kao zakašnjeli. To nije zanemarljiv procenat kad govorimo o isplatama u eurima. Trenutno radimo sa jednim eksternim API-jem za status letova. Pokušali smo da uvedemo jednostavna pravila za otkrivanje anomalija, ali lažni alarmi blokiraju legitimne isplate. Potreban nam je metod koji može da proceni verodostojnost dolaznih podataka pre nego što okidač aktivira isplatu — po mogućnosti u realnom vremenu, jer ceo smisao proizvoda je da korisnik dobije obaveštenje pre nego što napusti aerodrom. Imamo log svih prethodnih API poziva i isplata, što ukupno daje oko 340.000 unosa. Budžet za ovo nije neograničen — gledamo rešenje koje može da radi unutar naše postojeće infrastrukture, ne novi sistem od nule.

challenges.text: We want to price parametric festival-cancellation policies based on historical weather and event cancellation data, but we have fewer than 200 historical festival events in our database and standard actuarial methods need far more data points to produce stable loss curves.
challenges.detail: Razvijamo parametarsko osiguranje za organizatore open-air festivala: polisa se aktivira ako prognoza padavina premašuje prag u danima događaja, ili ako vlast zabrani održavanje zbog vremenskih uslova. Da bismo postavili cenu, trebaju nam stabilne krive gubitaka. Naša baza podataka sadrži nešto ispod 200 istorijskih festival-događaja u regionu sa pratećim vremenskim podacima — to je premalo za klasične aktuarske metode, krive su nestabilne i margine koje treba da naplatimo postaju nekonkurentne. Probali smo da dopunimo bazu podacima iz otvorenih izvora i novinskih arhiva, ali kvalitet i doslednost su neujednačeni. Razmišljamo o tome da iskoristimo meteorološke podatke šire — recimo statistiku ekstrema za svaku regiju i sezonu — pa da model gradimo odozdo prema gore umesto čisto iz istorije događaja. Nemamo kapacitet da to sami izvedemo do kraja, jer naš aktuarski tim broji dve osobe. Konkretan cilj: metodologija za cenovnik koja daje razumne intervale pouzdanosti čak i sa malim skupom istorijskih događaja, primenljiva na različite lokacije u regionu.

challenges.text: We need to appoint a licensed insurance intermediary in Austria to distribute through a Vienna-based travel platform, and the FMA licensing process has been stalled for seven months because our legal representative resigned.
challenges.detail: Potpisali smo ugovor o distribuciji sa bečkom platformom za rezervaciju putovanja ViennaJourney GmbH i trebalo je da krenemo u prodaju u prvom kvartalu 2024. Međutim, postupak dobijanja licence kod austrijskog regulatora FMA je u zastoju sedam meseci. Naš pravni zastupnik koji je vodio predmet podneo je ostavku prošlog leta i dokumentacija je ostala nedovršena. Pronašli smo novog savetnika, ali procedura kreće praktično ispočetka jer FMA traži određene dokumente overene od lica koje je prvobitno podnelo zahtev. Radi se o regulatornom, a ne tehničkom problemu — ali ima direktan uticaj na prihod jer je ViennaJourney GmbH uvrstio naš proizvod u plan za letnju sezonu. Ne tražimo prečice, tražimo nekog ko poznaje FMA proceduru iznutra i ko može da pomogne da složimo dokumentaciju na način koji neće biti vraćen po treći put. Vremenski pritisak postoji: ako ne dobijemo licencu do maja 2024, partner pomera integraciju za celu sezonu.

companies.plans: Do kraja 2025. planiramo da proširimo agro-liniju na Bugarsku i Rumuniju kroz partnerstvo sa regionalnim zadrugama, i da uvedemo novi okidač za osiguranje od mraza. companies.name: Kardiolink a.d.
companies.about:
Kardiolink a.d. has been designing and manufacturing cardiac monitoring devices in Novi Sad since 2004. We started as a small team of electrical engineers and cardiologists who believed that continuous ECG monitoring should not require a hospital stay. Twenty years later, we employ 112 people across hardware design, firmware, clinical affairs, and software, and our patches are used by cardiology clinics and remote patient monitoring programmes in fourteen EU countries.

Our core product is the KL-Patch line: single-use, adhesive ECG patches that patients wear for up to 72 hours while going about their normal lives. Clinicians receive processed reports through our cloud-based KardioPortal platform. We handle everything from electrode chemistry and PCB layout to the signal processing algorithms and the regulatory documentation that lets our devices reach patients legally.

What keeps us grounded is that we manufacture in-house at our Novi Sad facility. We control tolerances, can trace every component, and can respond to field feedback without waiting on a contract manufacturer. Our clinical team works directly with cardiologists at partner clinics to make sure what we ship is actually useful at the bedside, not just impressive on a datasheet. We are a mid-size company and intend to stay close to the product.
products: KL-Patch 72: 72-hour single-use adhesive ECG monitoring patch
KL-Patch 14: 14-day extended-wear cardiac event recorder
KardioPortal: cloud platform for ECG data management and clinical reporting
KL-Reader: clinic-side docking station and data upload terminal
Custom OEM patch manufacturing for third-party remote monitoring programmes
tech: ADS1293 and ADS1298 analog front-end ICs for ECG acquisition
nRF52840 SoC for Bluetooth Low Energy communication and firmware
FreeRTOS on ARM Cortex-M4 for embedded firmware
Lossless ECG compression using modified SZ algorithm
AWS S3 and Glacier tiered storage for signal archives
IEC 62304-compliant software lifecycle toolchain (Jira, Confluence, Polarion)
Altium Designer for PCB layout and design verification
Python and MATLAB for signal processing algorithm prototyping

challenges.text: Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz.
challenges.detail: The KL-Patch 72 runs on a 54 mAh lithium cell. At rest, current draw is manageable, but the moment Bluetooth is advertising or streaming, we see peaks that push daily consumption to 18 mAh. For an average patient that leaves about 18 mAh in reserve across three days, which is fine. The problem is active patients — people who trigger more frequent data syncs because they are moving and the device is flagging events. In a cardiology population that is not a small group. We have already tuned BLE advertising intervals and moved to BLE 5.0 long-range PHY for some use cases, and we switched to a lower-power MCU variant last year. We are now within a few milliamps of what we think we can achieve through firmware changes alone. We need someone who understands the full power budget — radio duty cycling, ADC configuration, memory access patterns — and can find where the remaining headroom is. The constraint is hard: sampling rate cannot drop below 250 Hz or the clinical validity of the signal is affected. We have instrumented reference hardware in our lab with a Keysight N6705C power analyzer and can provide full current profiles to anyone working on this.

challenges.text: We generate roughly 2 TB of raw ECG signal per month from field devices; our current lossless compression gives us only 3:1 ratio and storage costs at our cloud provider have reached €7,400 per month, which is unsustainable at the patient volume we are projecting for next year.
challenges.detail: Each KL-Patch 72 device generates roughly 900 MB of raw 16-bit ECG samples over its wear period at 250 Hz across three channels. We are deploying around 2,200 devices per month and growing. Our current pipeline applies a lossless compression step before upload, and the best we consistently achieve is 3:1, which still leaves us pushing about 2 TB to cloud storage each month. At €7,400 per month that is already a significant operating cost, and if we hit our projected 4,000 devices per month by Q2 next year the bill more than doubles. We looked at moving to lossy compression but our regulatory submission is built around lossless, so changing that requires a new clinical validation study and amendments to the technical file — not something we can do quickly. We also explored cold storage tiering and that saves maybe 15%, not enough. What we actually need is a better lossless algorithm that understands the structure of ECG signals: the quasi-periodic nature, the baseline wander, the noise characteristics of a wearable electrode. We have a labelled dataset of about 140,000 30-minute segments we can share under NDA for algorithm development and benchmarking.

challenges.text: Our CE MDR technical file was submitted eight months ago and the notified body has come back with 23 queries about our software lifecycle documentation under IEC 62304; we do not have in-house regulatory affairs staff experienced with the new MDR annexes and hiring one is taking longer than expected.
challenges.detail: We submitted our CE marking technical file under MDR in July last year. The notified body, Zertivo GmbH, came back four months later with 23 written queries. About 18 of the 23 concern our software lifecycle documentation under IEC 62304, specifically the traceability between our risk management records under ISO 14971 and the software safety classification rationale, and the completeness of our verification and validation activity records. We built our QMS years ago under the old MDD and have been adapting it incrementally, but the MDR annexes — particularly Annex I and the software-specific parts of Annex II — are much more demanding. We have two quality engineers on staff who are competent at our manufacturing QMS but have not worked through an MDR submission before at this level of detail. We posted a regulatory affairs manager role three months ago and have not found the right candidate. We need practical help drafting responses to these 23 queries and updating the underlying documentation. The notified body has given us a six-month window to respond before the file lapses. Missing that window means restarting the submission, which would cost us at minimum one full year and delay entry into two new national markets.

companies.plans: Kardiolink plans to launch the KL-Patch 14 in the German and Dutch markets following CE MDR certification and to expand KardioPortal with a structured reporting module aimed at high-volume cardiology outpatient departments. Over the following two years we intend to grow the device fleet to 6,000 active patches per month and bring cloud infrastructure costs back in line with 2022 levels.
companies.rd_capacity: We have twelve people working across hardware, firmware, and algorithm development, with a shared lab equipped for electronics prototyping, signal acquisition testing, and device-level EMC pre-compliance testing.
companies.past_collaborations: Between 2019 and 2021 Kardiolink worked with the engineering faculty in Subotica on a student project to evaluate alternative electrode materials, which informed the adhesive layer redesign in the KL-Patch 72 revision three.

companies.name: PravniPilot a.d.
companies.about:
PravniPilot a.d. was founded in 2012 in Subotica by a small team of practicing lawyers and software developers who were tired of spending hours manually searching court archives. We started with a simple keyword-search tool for Serbian civil cases and, over twelve years, grew that into a full AI-assisted research and case-prediction platform now used by 230 law firms in Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

Our platform ingests published court decisions, extracts key legal arguments, and gives lawyers a structured view of how similar disputes have been decided. The prediction module estimates probable outcome ranges for commercial, labor, and property disputes. We do not replace legal judgment — we give lawyers faster access to better evidence so their judgment is better informed.

Our development office sits inside NTP Novi Sad, where most of our engineering and data team works. The Subotica headquarters handles commercial, finance and client relations. Across both offices we employ 78 people, roughly half of them with legal backgrounds.

Our current customers range from two-partner boutique firms in Banja Luka to mid-size litigation practices in Zagreb and Belgrade. We have processed over two million court decisions and continue to add new documents daily. We are not the fastest-growing company in legal tech, but our retention rate — 91% of firms renew annually — tells us we are building something genuinely useful.

Case-outcome prediction module for commercial, labor and property disputes
Document annotation and summary tool with source citation
Court-decision bulk data export API for enterprise customers
Custom legal dataset licensing for insurers and financial institutions

PyTorch for transformer-based text classification
Elasticsearch for full-text document indexing

challenges.text: Our case-outcome prediction model achieves only 61% accuracy on commercial-dispute rulings from Serbian courts, which is barely better than a lawyer's gut feeling; we suspect the problem is that our training set has only 9,000 labelled decisions and courts don't publish enough structured data.
challenges.detail: Our prediction model was trained on roughly 9,000 labeled commercial-dispute decisions from Serbian courts. At 61% accuracy it is not meaningfully better than what an experienced lawyer estimates from memory. We have tried basic data augmentation and have experimented with pre-trained multilingual models fine-tuned on our corpus, but neither moved the needle past 63% in internal tests. The core problem is data volume: Serbian courts do not publish decisions in a consistent machine-readable format, so each document requires significant cleaning before it can be labeled. We have one full-time data engineer and two part-time annotators working on this. We estimate we need at least 40,000 clean, labeled decisions to reach accuracy worth advertising. We are open to exploring transfer learning from Croatian or Bosnian court data, semi-supervised labeling, or better feature extraction from judgment text. A good outcome would be reaching 75% accuracy on a held-out test set within 12 months, which would let us market the prediction feature with honest confidence intervals rather than quietly downplaying it.

challenges.text: We are trying to raise a €2.5 million Series A round to fund expansion into the German legal market but all three venture funds we spoke to in Q1 said our cap table structure is too messy from the 2019 convertible note round; we need legal restructuring advice, not technology.
challenges.detail: In 2019 we issued a convertible note to bridge a funding gap. The terms were set in a hurry and the resulting cap table now shows overlapping anti-dilution provisions that make it hard for a new lead investor to model their ownership cleanly. We have spoken with three regional venture funds this year, all of whom expressed interest in the product but pulled back after reviewing our shareholder agreement. Our target is a €2.5 million Series A to fund a German market entry, including translation of the platform and local business development hiring. We need a corporate lawyer with cross-border experience in Serbian and EU startup financing to help us clean up the note terms, renegotiate with the existing noteholders, and produce a cap table that a German or Austrian fund can read without confusion. This is not a technology problem. We have a moderate budget for legal advisory work and a soft deadline of Q3 this year if we want to start German operations before end of 2025.

challenges.text: Law firm users copy our AI-generated research summaries directly into briefs without reading them, and twice this year the summaries contained an outdated precedent; we need a way to attach confidence scores and source provenance to every generated sentence.
challenges.detail: We generate paragraph-level summaries of relevant court decisions and legal arguments. Several law firm users have told us they paste these summaries directly into draft briefs without checking the source. Twice this year a summary referenced a precedent that had been overturned or amended, and in one case a firm submitted a brief containing the outdated citation before catching the error. We take this seriously. What we want to build is a system that attaches a confidence score and a direct source link to every sentence or claim in a generated summary, so a lawyer can see at a glance whether a statement is based on one decision or fifty, and how recent the most recent supporting case is. We have experimented with simple retrieval-augmented generation, but sentence-level provenance tracking in a multilingual legal context is harder than it looks. We have budget for one additional engineer and are willing to explore collaboration with external research groups. The hard requirement is that the solution works inside our existing React interface without requiring a workflow change for the lawyer.

challenges.text: We store full-text court decisions for three jurisdictions and search response time has degraded from 0.4 seconds to 3.1 seconds since we crossed 2 million documents; our database engineers say we need a fundamentally different indexing architecture.
challenges.detail: When we crossed two million documents in our Elasticsearch cluster last autumn, average search response time climbed from 0.4 seconds to 3.1 seconds. Our two database engineers have tried index sharding, query caching and hardware upgrades, and we got the time down to 2.4 seconds, but that is still unacceptable for a tool lawyers use dozens of times a day during trial preparation. The problem is that our index was designed for a corpus of a few hundred thousand documents and has not been fundamentally rethought since. We are adding roughly 15,000 new documents per month across three jurisdictions, so the situation will keep getting worse. We are open to replacing Elasticsearch with a different architecture, moving to a vector-based semantic search layer, or a hybrid approach, but any solution must support our existing boolean filter queries, multilingual text and our API contract with enterprise customers. Downtime during migration is a serious concern — we cannot afford more than a four-hour maintenance window. Budget for infrastructure changes is available but we would prefer a phased approach.

companies.plans: PravniPilot intends to launch a German-language pilot of its research platform with at least five German law firms by mid-2026, contingent on completing the Series A round. In parallel, the company plans to release a public confidence-scoring API for legal summaries that smaller legal-tech vendors in the region can license.
companies.rd_capacity: Our development team of 14 engineers and two data scientists can allocate roughly two days per week to collaborative research work, provided any research output can be integrated directly into the production codebase.
companies.past_collaborations: PravniPilot ran a six-month data-labeling project with a Novi Sad-based language annotation firm, LinguaNova d.o.o., in 2022 to produce a cleaned subset of Croatian court decisions, but has no current active research partnerships.

companies.name: Suncokret Eko d.o.o.
companies.sector: Cleantech — biomass and organic waste valorisation
companies.about:
Suncokret Eko d.o.o. was founded in 2017 in Novi Sad by a small group of agricultural engineers and process technicians who wanted to do something practical with the mountains of sunflower husks and maize cobs left behind every harvest season in Vojvodina. We started with a single pellet press in a rented hall near the Danube and now operate a full processing line at the NTP Novi Sad campus with 31 people on staff.

We buy agricultural residues directly from farms and food-processing plants across the region, dry and sort them, and convert them into two main products: pressed pellet fuel sold to district heating operators and private households, and biochar used as a soil amendment and carbon-sequestration material. Our domestic heating customers include several municipal utility companies in Serbia and a growing number of commercial greenhouse operators in Hungary and Romania. On the biochar side we are working toward export sales in Germany and the Netherlands.

What separates us from larger biomass processors is that we stay close to the feedstock supply chain. Our head of procurement, Milica Vranić, maintains direct contracts with fourteen farms, which gives us visibility on quality before material arrives at the gate. Our process lead, Dragan Ostojić, has run more than two hundred pyrolysis batches and keeps detailed logs that we use to tune every run. We are not the biggest operation in the region, but we know our material well.
products: Wood-free biomass pellets (ENplus-equivalent grade) from sunflower husks and maize cobs
Agricultural biochar for soil amendment and carbon sequestration
Custom pelletising service for third-party agricultural waste streams
Bulk biochar supply for industrial composting and land reclamation projects
Carbon removal documentation support package for biochar buyers seeking credit eligibility
tech: Rotary drum drying for feedstock moisture control
Hammer-mill particle-size reduction and screening
Flat-die and ring-die pellet presses
Slow-pyrolysis reactor (batch, 400–700 °C operating range)
Proximate and ultimate analysis of biochar (fixed carbon, ash, volatile matter)
Feedstock moisture monitoring with in-line NIR sensors

ISO 17225 pellet quality testing protocols

challenges.text: Our biochar product tests at around 55% fixed carbon but customers in Germany need at least 70% for soil-amendment certification; we've tried raising pyrolysis temperature but that cuts yield by nearly a third and makes the economics fall apart.
challenges.detail: Our biochar consistently comes out with around 55% fixed carbon when we run the pyrolyser at 500–520 °C, which is where our yield is commercially acceptable. Buyers in Germany and the Netherlands need at least 70% fixed carbon to qualify under soil-amendment certification schemes. We have pushed the temperature up to 650 °C and beyond in trials, and we do hit the 70% threshold, but the mass yield drops from roughly 28% to under 20%, which means we need about 40% more raw material to fill the same order. At current feedstock and energy costs that wipes out the price premium we get for certified biochar. We have also tried extending the hold time at lower temperatures rather than raising the peak, but the gains in fixed carbon are modest. We have two years of batch logs covering temperature profiles, feedstock moisture, particle size and output quality that we can share. We need a way to improve fixed-carbon content without either wrecking yield or requiring capital we do not have for a new reactor. A good outcome would be a process adjustment we can test on our existing equipment within six months.

challenges.text: We want to enrol our biochar in the European Biochar Certificate scheme to sell carbon removal credits but the documentation requirements are in German and English and keep changing; we've already spent six months on paperwork without submitting a complete application.
challenges.detail: The European Biochar Certificate is the main route for us to register carbon removal credits and charge a premium to buyers who need documented carbon sequestration. We have been trying to prepare an application for almost a year. The scheme requires detailed chain-of-custody records, feedstock declarations, specific lab analyses, and a written quality management description that maps to their framework document, which is updated periodically. Our team speaks Serbian and we have one colleague, Jovana Filipović, who handles correspondence in English, but the technical language in the EBC framework is not straightforward even for native speakers. We have collected most of the required lab data and we have roughly 18 months of production records. What we are missing is someone who can read the current framework critically, identify exactly what gaps we still have in our documentation, and help us write the quality management section in a way that satisfies the auditors. We have a small budget set aside for this, around 4,000 EUR, and we would like to submit a complete application before the end of the year.

challenges.text: Our pellet press breaks down about once a month because the sunflower husk feedstock has inconsistent moisture and particle size coming from different suppliers; downtime costs us roughly 15,000 EUR per incident when we have delivery commitments.
challenges.detail: Our pellet press line goes down roughly once a month. The root cause is almost always the same: sunflower husk material arriving with moisture content or particle size outside the range the press can handle. When moisture is above 14% the dies clog; when there is too much fine dust mixed with coarser pieces the compression is uneven and we get bearing failures. Different suppliers deliver material that can vary from 8% to 22% moisture and from fine powder to chunks over 15 mm in the same delivery. Our current process is to check a sample at intake and reject loads that look bad, but our in-line NIR sensor only covers moisture and is not reliable below 10% or above 18%, and we have no automated particle-size check at all. Each breakdown costs us around 15,000 EUR in lost production, emergency maintenance and contract penalties. We have looked at pre-conditioning equipment, specifically a secondary hammer mill and a conditioning mixer, but we have not been able to confirm whether the spec we are considering would actually stabilise output enough to prevent failures. We need a clearer picture of what incoming feedstock variance is acceptable and what pre-processing steps would bring our current suppliers' material inside that range.

companies.plans: Suncokret Eko is expanding pyrolysis capacity with a second batch reactor expected to be operational by mid-2026, targeting a combined biochar output of 400 tonnes per year. We are also exploring co-processing of food-industry digestate with our existing agricultural residue streams to diversify feedstock supply.
companies.rd_capacity: We have two technically trained staff who can run controlled production trials and maintain detailed process logs, but we do not have dedicated research personnel or laboratory equipment beyond basic moisture and proximate-analysis tools.
companies.past_collaborations: We completed a six-month feedstock characterisation project in 2022 with the Institute for Food Technology in Novi Sad (FINS) to benchmark the energy content of regional sunflower husk varieties.

companies.name: Elekron Sistemi a.d.
companies.about: Elekron Sistemi a.d. was founded in 1987 in Subotica by the Vukičević family, who started by building custom relay control panels for local factories. Over the following decades the company grew into a recognised supplier of ruggedised electronic control panels and remote terminal units for municipal water, heating, and waste-water operators across Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. In 2014 the founding family transferred ownership to an employee trust, and today the 117 people who work here are also the owners. That structure suits us: decisions are made by people who understand the hardware and stand behind every unit that leaves Subotica. Our sheet-metal workshop bends and welds roughly 2,400 panels a year entirely in-house. Our RTU product line communicates over licensed radio, GSM, and, since 2021, LoRaWAN — a direction we are pushing hard because municipal clients need affordable ways to connect meters that were installed before wireless was an option. We hold framework contracts with seven municipal utilities and work through regional integrators in Sarajevo and Skopje. Quality certification to IEC 61439 and a service team that can reach most Western Balkans sites within 24 hours are what clients mention most when they explain why they keep reordering.

challenges.text: We are retrofitting legacy water and heat meters for three municipal clients in Bosnia and North Macedonia with our LoRaWAN collar device, but the received signal strength inside basement meter rooms is between -120 and -125 dBm, which is at the edge of our gateway sensitivity — about 9% of readings are missing per day and the clients are threatening penalty clauses after six months of missed SLA.
challenges.detail: We are fitting our LoRaWAN collar device onto existing water and heat meters in basement plant rooms for three municipal clients — two in Bosnia and one in North Macedonia. The problem is signal. Measured RSSI inside these rooms runs between -120 and -125 dBm, right at the edge of what our gateways can reliably decode. We are using SF12 already, which is the slowest spreading factor and gives us the best link budget, but we are still losing around 9% of daily readings. The SLA we signed requires 99% daily read success, so we are in breach and have been for six months. We have tried repositioning gateway antennas on rooftops and adding one repeater node per building with limited improvement. We do not have budget for a full gateway infrastructure overhaul — the contracts are fixed-price. What we need is either a way to recover more packets from weak signals, a smarter retransmission scheme that fits within the duty-cycle limits, or a low-cost way to extend coverage into these specific rooms. A good outcome is getting missed reads below 1% without replacing the gateways or re-running cables.

challenges.text: Our sheet-metal enclosure workshop in Subotica produces around 2,400 panels a year; we bend and weld everything in-house but we are seeing a 6% rework rate on powder-coated parts because weld spatter creates surface defects that only appear after coating — we lose roughly 140,000 dinars per month in rework labour and materials.
challenges.detail: Our panel enclosures go through MIG welding before powder coating, and we have a persistent rework problem. Weld spatter — tiny metal balls that stick to the sheet surface — is not always visible before the part goes into the coating oven. After coating the spatter shows up as raised bumps or pinholes and the part has to be stripped, re-ground, re-primed, and re-coated. We track rework per batch and the rate has sat at around 6% for three years. That translates to roughly 140,000 dinars a month in extra labour and materials, not counting the scheduling delays when a batch comes back. We have tried tightening welding parameters, switching to an anti-spatter spray, and adding a manual inspection step before priming, but the manual check catches maybe half the defective parts. Our workshop supervisor, Branimir Talić, thinks the real issue is inconsistency between welders on different shifts. We have no automated inspection equipment. We are open to any approach — sensor-based, vision-based, process change — as long as it fits in a workshop that runs two shifts and cannot afford long production stoppages for installation. Cutting the rework rate to under 1.5% would recover most of the cost.

challenges.text: We want to expand into Romania and Bulgaria but our sales team of five people has no experience with public procurement rules there — we have lost two tenders already because we submitted the wrong notarial documents and missed a local-content clause we did not know existed.
challenges.detail: We want to sell our RTU and control panel products directly to municipal utilities in Romania and Bulgaria rather than through local resellers who take a large margin. Both countries run public tenders through their national e-procurement portals. We have a sales team of five, all experienced with Serbian and regional procurement under UNCITRAL-style rules, but Romanian and Bulgarian tender documents use different notarial certification formats, translated attestation requirements, and, in two tenders we entered, local-content or EU-origin documentation we were not aware of. We lost both tenders on administrative grounds before technical evaluation even started. We do not have a local legal partner in either country yet. We have budget for a short consultancy engagement and we are willing to pay a success fee on a first contract win. What we need is either a structured guide to the documentation requirements for each country, or a contact who can review our tender packs before submission. A realistic target is winning one contract in Romania or Bulgaria within 18 months.

challenges.text: The RTU firmware we ship has grown to 340,000 lines of C code over 20 years and nobody on the team fully understands the interrupt-handling layer anymore — we had two field failures in the last year caused by race conditions that took an average of 11 weeks each to reproduce and fix, which is unacceptable for critical infrastructure clients.
challenges.detail: Our main RTU firmware is a C codebase that has been added to by many different engineers since 2003. It now runs to about 340,000 lines and the interrupt-handling layer was written by two engineers who have since retired. We had two separate field failures last year — both traced back to race conditions where an interrupt fired during a flash-write operation and corrupted a register. Each one took an average of 11 weeks to reproduce in the lab because the fault only appeared under specific timing conditions with real hardware attached. That is unacceptable for clients running water or heating distribution. We have no formal concurrency model documented, no static analysis in the CI pipeline, and our current team is not confident modifying the interrupt layer. We are not in a position to rewrite the firmware from scratch — the product is in active production and we have contractual obligations. What we need is a method or toolset to find latent race conditions without a full rewrite, and some kind of structured documentation of the existing interrupt behaviour so future engineers can work on it safely. Budget is limited but the risk of another field failure is the bigger concern.

companies.plans: Elekron Sistemi intends to release a second-generation LoRaWAN collar with an integrated signal-boost relay option and to qualify the product line for sale in Romania and Bulgaria by the end of 2026. We are also evaluating whether to bring a small electronics assembly line in-house to reduce dependence on contract PCB assemblers in Novi Sad.
companies.rd_capacity: We have four engineers who can dedicate part of their time to a development collaboration, plus access to our production hardware, field-test sites at three municipal utilities, and a small lab in Subotica with oscilloscopes, protocol analysers, and environmental test chambers.
companies.past_collaborations: We completed a two-year product-development agreement with Integra Automatika d.o.o. from Novi Sad between 2019 and 2021 covering firmware portability across two RTU hardware revisions.

companies.name: LinguaBot d.o.o.
companies.about: LinguaBot d.o.o. was started in 2020 by three engineers who had spent years watching Serbian-language customer support run on copy-pasted email templates and overloaded call centres. We build conversational AI products specifically for Serbian-speaking users, which sounds narrow until you realise almost no one else bothers to do it properly. Our first client was a regional bank in Vojvodina; today we serve four banks and two telecoms providers across Serbia, handling roughly 140,000 chat sessions per month. Our team of 22 people sits inside the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad — mostly engineers, with a small product team and two computational linguists who focus exclusively on Serbian morphology and dialect variation. What makes us different is that we do not drop a generic multilingual model on top of a client's FAQ and call it done. We maintain our own annotated Serbian-language datasets, we run our own fine-tuning pipelines, and we treat morphological variation and script mixing as first-class engineering problems rather than edge cases. Clients stay with us because the bot actually understands what their customers type, not just the textbook version of it.

challenges.text: Our search misses answers because Serbian words change form (e.g. 'kartica', 'karticu', 'karticom') and users mix Latin and Cyrillic.
challenges.detail: Serbian is a heavily inflected language, so a single noun like 'kartica' (card) appears as 'karticu', 'karticom', 'kartice', 'karticama' depending on case, and verbs shift even more. On top of that, our users freely switch between Latin and Cyrillic script mid-sentence — sometimes mid-word in typos. Our current Elasticsearch setup uses a basic stemmer that was built for Croatian and misses a significant share of Serbian-specific forms. We have measured this: in a sample of 12,000 real support queries from one bank client, about 18% returned no useful result, and our analysis traced more than half of those misses directly to morphological mismatch or script confusion. We have tried adding synonym lists and a simple script-normalisation step, but maintaining those lists manually does not scale as clients add new product terminology every quarter. We have a labelled query-response dataset of around 85,000 pairs across all clients, and our two in-house linguists can annotate or validate proposed solutions. We need an approach that handles lemmatisation or indexing in a way that is accurate for Serbian, tolerates script mixing automatically, and can be updated when new vocabulary arrives without a full re-index. A good outcome is getting that 18% miss rate below 5% and keeping it there with a manageable maintenance process. Budget for tooling or data work is modest — around 8,000 EUR — and we want something testable within six months.

challenges.text: Clients want the bot on the phone too; speech recognition for Serbian is poor on call audio.
challenges.detail: Three of our bank clients have asked us to put the bot on their inbound phone lines by the end of 2027, and one telecom client has written it into a contract renewal that goes up for review in early 2027. The problem is that Serbian automatic speech recognition is genuinely poor on real call-centre audio: background noise, regional accents, fast speech, and the particular compression artifacts that come from telephony codecs all combine to produce word-error rates that make the transcript nearly unusable for intent detection. We tested two widely used commercial ASR APIs last year — neither is designed for Serbian — and word-error rates on a 300-call sample were above 38%, which is too high for reliable downstream understanding. We have a corpus of about 1,200 anonymised and consented call recordings from one client, covering a range of speaker ages and regional accents, but that is not enough to fine-tune a robust model from scratch on our own. We have four ML engineers, but none of them has deep experience in speech model training specifically. We are not expecting a production-ready ASR system from a collaboration — what we need is a clear view of what data we would need to collect, what modelling approach is realistic given our constraints, and ideally a small proof-of-concept that shows whether fine-tuning an existing multilingual model on our 1,200 recordings moves the needle enough to justify the larger data-collection effort. Timeline is firm because of the contract.

challenges.text: Micro firms often have under a year of history; our scoring rejects good borrowers.
challenges.detail: A large share of the businesses that apply to us have been operating for under twelve months. They do not have enough transaction history for our current scoring model to form a reliable view, so the model either rejects them outright or assigns such a high risk tier that the interest rate we would need to charge makes the loan unattractive. We know from manual reviews that some of these firms are well-run — the owner has relevant sector experience, the cash flow pattern looks healthy, the business type carries low historical default rates — but we cannot encode that judgment at scale. We have tried adding sector-average benchmarks as proxy features and experimenting with alternative data like utility payments, but neither moved the needle enough to change our approval rate on this segment. Our data team has a labeled dataset of roughly 400 young-firm applications where we have the eventual outcome, so there is something to work with, though it is not large. We need a way to get better signal from thin-file applicants without loosening standards in a way that raises our default rate. A good outcome would be approving 15 to 20 percent more young-firm applicants while keeping defaults within our current band.

challenges.text: The central bank wants every automated decision explained.
challenges.detail: The National Bank of Serbia has made clear that every automated credit decision we issue must be accompanied by a plain-language explanation that a borrower can understand and, if they wish, challenge. Right now our main scoring model is a gradient-boosted ensemble that performs well but produces outputs that are hard to explain in plain terms. We have experimented with SHAP values to identify which features drove a particular decision, and we do generate a short internal summary, but that summary is written in technical language that most borrowers find confusing, and our compliance officer, Dragana Vukić, is not satisfied it meets the spirit of the regulator's guidance. We have a hard requirement to have a compliant explanation format in place before we expand to North Macedonia, where similar rules apply. The explanation needs to be generated automatically at decision time, stored alongside the decision record, and rendered in the borrower portal in Serbian and, for the expansion, Macedonian. Budget for this work is modest — we are not looking for a research project, we need something that works reliably in production within about six months.

challenges.text: Our biggest German client is asking us to add an AI-driven product recommendation engine to their e-commerce platform; we have 18 months of transaction history across 340,000 SKUs but none of our current developers have the machine learning depth to build a production-grade model — we lost the last tender because a Polish competitor could show a working prototype.
challenges.detail: One of our largest German clients, a regional e-commerce distributor, has asked us to build a product recommendation engine that runs inside their existing platform. They have given us read access to 18 months of transaction records covering around 340,000 active SKUs, plus some basic customer segmentation data. The problem is that none of our current developers have built and deployed a machine learning model at this scale before. We ran a small experiment using an open-source collaborative filtering library and the results were not good enough to show the client. We lost an earlier tender on a similar brief because a competitor from Poland was able to demonstrate a working prototype in the pitch meeting — we could not. The client has given us roughly 18 months before they would consider moving the work elsewhere. We need someone who can help us design a model architecture that can actually go into production, train on the data we already have, and connect to our existing Node.js back end. We are also open to a transfer of knowledge so our own team can maintain and retrain the model going forward rather than being dependent on outside help indefinitely.

challenges.text: We onboard roughly four new EU clients a year, and every single one requires us to sign their own data processing agreement under GDPR; our lead developer is spending almost two weeks per contract just reviewing clauses, which is pulling him off billable work and we can't afford an in-house lawyer.
challenges.detail: Every new EU client we sign requires us to agree to their own data processing agreement before we can start work. The language in these contracts varies significantly — some are straightforward, some include clauses around sub-processor lists, audit rights, and data residency that need careful reading before we sign. Right now our lead developer, Marko Ilić, is the person who reviews all of them because he has the most experience with how our systems actually handle data. He estimates he spends close to two weeks of billable time per contract on this review, which at our project margins is genuinely painful. We have tried using a standard template from a Serbian IT industry association as a reference point, but clients do not accept our version — they want us to sign theirs. We cannot justify a full-time in-house lawyer for four contracts a year. We are looking for a practical way to speed up this review process and reduce the burden on our technical staff, whether that is a structured checklist, a clause-comparison tool, or a repeatable workflow that someone without a legal background can actually follow.

challenges.text: Our CI/CD pipeline runs full regression on every push and the test suite now takes 4.5 hours; developers are merging less often and bugs are slipping through because people skip the wait, so our defect escape rate to production has gone up from 2% to 9% over the last six months.
challenges.detail: Our test suite has grown alongside our client base and now takes about four and a half hours to run end to end. We run it on every push to the main branch via GitLab CI/CD on a self-managed runner cluster hosted on AWS. The tests themselves are a mix of Jest unit tests and Playwright end-to-end scenarios that were written over several years without much central coordination, so there is significant overlap between them. The practical result is that developers have started merging less frequently and in some cases are bypassing the full run by targeting only the subset of tests that cover their immediate change. Over the last six months our defect escape rate to production has climbed from around 2 percent to around 9 percent, and we have had two client-facing incidents that we attribute directly to this. We have tried parallelising some of the Playwright tests across multiple runner instances and brought the time down from about six hours, but four and a half hours is still too long to maintain good development habits. We need help thinking about how to restructure the suite — potentially through test selection, better parallelisation, or identifying and removing redundant coverage — without reducing actual confidence in what we ship.

challenges.text: Three Dutch clients want their dashboards to show carbon footprint per shipment in real time, but we have no in-house expertise on emission factor databases or lifecycle calculation standards — we are guessing at methodology and one client has already flagged that our numbers don't match their own consultant's figures.
challenges.detail: Three of our Dutch logistics clients have asked us to display carbon footprint figures per shipment on their operational dashboards. We built the basic display layer without difficulty, but the underlying calculation is where we are struggling. We do not have anyone on the team with a background in emissions accounting or lifecycle assessment, so we researched publicly available emission factor tables and built a calculation ourselves. One client then compared our figures against a report produced by their own sustainability consultant and found meaningful discrepancies — in one case our per-kilometre figure for road freight was around 30 percent lower than the consultant's. We do not know whether the gap is in the emission factor source, the allocation method, or somewhere in our load and distance logic. The clients are not asking for certified calculations, but they do need figures they can use in their own reporting without embarrassment. We need someone who understands the relevant calculation standards — particularly around freight transport — and can help us build a methodology that is defensible and consistent, and ideally point us toward the right data sources so we can maintain it ourselves as emission factor tables are updated.

companies.plans: Velago plans to grow its logistics client base in Germany and the Netherlands over the next two years, with a focus on clients who need ongoing platform development rather than one-off project work. We are also actively looking at adding data and analytics capability to our service offering so we can handle a wider range of client requirements in-house.

challenges.text: We run manual penetration tests that take our team about two weeks per engagement; clients are asking for continuous testing and retest after patches, but at our size we simply can't bill enough hours to make that sustainable — we need a way to automate at least the reconnaissance and vulnerability enumeration phases.
challenges.detail: A standard engagement for us runs about two weeks: a few days of reconnaissance and enumeration, then active testing, then a reporting phase. That rhythm works when a client wants a point-in-time audit once a year. The problem is that several clients — especially the two municipalities and a regional medical supply company — have started asking us to retest after they apply patches, and one of them mentioned they want something closer to monthly checks on their external attack surface. We simply do not have the hours to bill that at our current rates and stay profitable. We have tried writing Bash scripts to partially automate the initial scanning phase, and that saves maybe two hours per engagement, but it is fragile and hard to maintain. We need a more reliable pipeline that can run scheduled reconnaissance and vulnerability enumeration, flag changes since the last scan, and hand results to our testers in a structured format. If we could cut the first phase from four days to one, we could take on retest work without adding headcount. Budget for tooling or a development collaboration is limited — roughly 3,000 to 5,000 euros — but we are open to a research arrangement where the output is a working prototype.

challenges.text: Two municipalities hired us and then couldn't act on our findings because their IT staff didn't understand the remediation steps; we'd like a structured training programme we could sell alongside the audit, but writing curriculum and measuring knowledge retention is not something we know how to do.
challenges.detail: After finishing audits for two municipal clients, Opština Kanjiza and a second municipality we are not naming publicly, we delivered detailed reports and then watched nothing get fixed for three months. When we followed up, the honest answer from their IT coordinators was that the remediation steps read like a foreign language to them. We ran two informal afternoon sessions explaining the findings in plain terms, and that actually helped — one municipality patched four out of seven critical issues within a month afterward. So we know training works, but right now we deliver it informally and for free because we have no product to charge for. We would like to build a short structured programme — probably four to six modules — that we can sell as an add-on to any audit. The challenge is we do not know how to design curriculum properly, how to test whether people retained anything, or how to keep the material updated as the threat landscape changes. We have the technical content in our heads. We need help turning it into something repeatable and measurable. A good outcome would be a pilot programme we could test with one municipality client by the end of this year.

challenges.text: We've been trying for five months to register as a certified auditor under the Serbian Information Security Law so we can bid on public procurement contracts, but the paperwork at the Ministry keeps bouncing back for minor formal reasons and we don't know how to fix it.
challenges.detail: Serbian law on information security requires that organisations in certain sectors use certified auditors for their mandatory audits. That certification would open public procurement to us, which currently we cannot bid on at all. We applied to the Ministry five months ago and have had the application returned three times, each time with a short note citing a formal deficiency. The first return was about the formatting of an attached document. The second was about a reference number on a supporting form. The third cited an unclear clause about professional experience documentation. We have tried reading the relevant rulebook ourselves and consulting a general business lawyer in Subotica who was honest enough to say she does not know this specific regulatory area well. We are not looking for legal advice in the strict sense — we just need someone who has successfully navigated this specific process and can look at our application package and tell us concretely what is wrong. A good outcome is a submitted application that does not come back. We would like to resolve this within the next three months because there is a municipal procurement round opening in the autumn that we want to be eligible for.
