challenges.text: Our telematics black-box records speed, braking and cornering, but we still price everyone in the same age-vehicle bracket the same way — we need a model that actually translates raw trip events into a per-driver risk score we can price off.
challenges.detail: Every trip our black-box records produces a stream of events — speed samples every two seconds, hard-brake flags, sharp-cornering flags, night-driving flags. We store all of it in our PostgreSQL warehouse, so the raw material is there: roughly 380 million trip-event rows covering the last four years and about 9,400 active devices. The problem is that our pricing team of four has never had the time or the specific background to turn those rows into something the rating engine can use. Right now we group drivers only by age band and vehicle category, which means a cautious 24-year-old pays the same as an aggressive one. We tried building a simple points-based score in-house last year but the loss ratio on the telematics segment barely moved. What we want is a scoring method that takes the raw events, accounts for trip length and road type as far as we can infer it, and outputs a single per-driver number we can map directly onto a loading or discount. Our target is to have something running in the rating engine before the next annual product filing, which is due in the first quarter of 2026. Budget for outside help is modest but real — we can provide full access to the anonymised trip data under a data-processing agreement.

challenges.text: Property claims for hail damage on Vojvodina farms are costing us about 18% more per claim than our pricing assumed; we believe we're underestimating exposure because we don't know how to map hail intensity at field level.
challenges.detail: Hail claims on Vojvodina farm property have been running about 18% above our loss assumption for the past three summers. Our current approach is to rate by municipality and apply a single hail loading per municipality, but Vojvodina hailstorms are narrow and fast-moving — a storm can devastate one village and leave the farm two kilometres away untouched. We do receive daily gridded weather data from MeteoVoj d.o.o. at a five-kilometre resolution, but we have not been able to link that data reliably to individual policy locations because a large share of our farm addresses are stored only at the settlement level, not as coordinates. We have tried overlaying the MeteoVoj grid manually in QGIS for the worst claim years, and the patterns look promising, but turning that into something that feeds the pricing model automatically is beyond what our team can do alone. A good outcome would be a method that takes our policy locations, matches them to hail intensity estimates at field level, and tells us which parts of our portfolio are priced too low. We have three full claim years with geo-tagged loss data for about 1,200 farm policies to work with.

challenges.text: We're trying to enter the Romanian market but the local regulator is asking for a Solvency II internal model validation report and we don't have the actuarial staff to produce one — our pricing team has four people.
challenges.detail: We submitted our Romanian branch application in late 2023 and the regulator has come back asking for an internal model validation report under Solvency II. This was not unexpected, but we underestimated how much work it involves. Our pricing team is four actuaries, two of whom joined in the last eighteen months and are still working toward their full fellowship exams. The remaining two are fully occupied with Serbia and Bosnia product filings. We have a standard formula model running for our Serbian regulatory returns, so we have the capital model concept — the gap is the formal validation documentation, the backtesting of loss distributions and the narrative that explains why the model is appropriate for our business mix. The Romanian portfolio we are proposing is small: private motor and urban apartment property only, capped at 5,000 policies in year one. We are not looking for someone to rebuild our model; we need someone who understands the Solvency II validation framework and can work with our two senior actuaries to produce a report the regulator will accept. We are targeting submission by October 2025, so the work would need to start by May at the latest.

challenges.text: We maintain BI dashboards for nine German manufacturing clients and each month we spend roughly 400 analyst-hours cleaning and reconciling data from SAP, legacy MES systems and spreadsheets before any report can go out — we need to automate that pipeline but the schemas change with every client upgrade.
challenges.detail: We run monthly BI reporting for nine German manufacturing clients. Every report cycle starts the same way: our analysts pull data from each client's SAP system, one or two legacy MES platforms, and a collection of Excel files that shop-floor supervisors maintain outside any formal system. Reconciling all of that takes roughly 400 analyst-hours per month across the team. The core problem is that client schemas change constantly — an SAP upgrade, a new production line, a change in how a plant codes its cost centers — and our existing ETL scripts break without warning. We have tried building more defensive pipelines in Airflow with schema-validation steps, and that caught some breakage earlier, but it still requires a human to diagnose and fix each mismatch. We have the raw data, we have access to client systems, and we have two senior data engineers who understand the domain well. What we need is a way to detect schema drift automatically and adapt mappings without full manual rewrites each time. A good result would be cutting that 400-hour monthly burden by at least half while keeping report accuracy at current levels.

challenges.text: A Dutch client processes personal data of 80,000 customers through our hosted platform; after their internal audit flagged a gap in our data-residency documentation, we've been asked to achieve ISO 27001 certification within nine months or lose the contract, and we've never done a formal ISMS implementation.
challenges.detail: One of our Dutch clients, a mid-sized packaging manufacturer, runs their customer management and order processing through a platform we host on Azure in the Amsterdam region. Their internal audit team reviewed our data-handling documentation earlier this year and found that our records on data residency, access controls and incident response procedures were not formalized to a standard they could show to their own regulators. They have given us nine months to achieve ISO 27001 certification or they will move the platform in-house. That contract represents roughly 12 percent of our annual revenue. We have never implemented a formal Information Security Management System. We understand the technical controls well enough — we already run encryption at rest, role-based access and regular backups — but we have no documented risk register, no formal asset inventory, no supplier assessment process, and no internal audit cycle. We have one IT security officer on staff who handles day-to-day access management but has not led a certification project. Budget for external support is available but not unlimited. A good outcome is certification within the deadline with processes our team can actually maintain afterward.

challenges.text: Our junior consultants take on average 11 months to reach billable productivity; we lose about €60k per head in that ramp period and attrition at month 14 means we rarely recoup it.
challenges.detail: We hire junior consultants and developers from universities in Novi Sad and Belgrade every year. On paper this is straightforward: we take graduates, train them on SAP integration, our internal tooling and client communication standards, and after a ramp period they carry billable work. In practice the ramp takes an average of eleven months before someone is generating enough billable output to cover their cost. We have calculated that we absorb roughly sixty thousand euros per head during that period in salary, supervisor time and client relationship risk. The bigger problem is that a meaningful share of those staff leave around month fourteen — right after they have become productive — typically for a Western European employer or a larger tech company. So we carry the full ramp cost and rarely get more than a few months of return. We have tried a structured mentoring program and a revised onboarding curriculum, which shortened some early ramp stages, but has not moved the overall number much. We want to understand whether the bottleneck is curriculum design, the way we assign early project work, or something else, and then build a training approach that is repeatable and measurable.

challenges.text: Three Austrian clients asked us to add natural-language querying to their BI dashboards so non-technical managers can ask questions in German and get correct SQL-backed charts; our test with an off-the-shelf LLM produced wrong aggregations in roughly 40% of finance queries.
challenges.detail: Three of our Austrian manufacturing clients want their managers to be able to type a question in plain German — something like 'what was our rejection rate on line three last quarter compared to the previous year' — and get back a correct chart without involving an analyst. We ran a pilot using an off-the-shelf large language model connected to one client's SQL database. The model produced plausible-looking queries, but when we checked the outputs against manually prepared reports, roughly forty percent of finance-related questions returned wrong aggregations — incorrect groupings, missing filters, misunderstood date ranges. The problem is not the language understanding; the model handles German phrasing reasonably well. The problem is that our clients' data models are complex and underdocumented, and the model has no reliable way to know which tables and columns actually mean what the business user intends. We have the schemas, some data dictionaries of varying quality, and samples of analyst-written queries that we know are correct. We need an approach that uses that existing material to constrain query generation reliably. A good outcome is a system where finance managers can run routine queries without analyst involvement and the error rate on those queries is below five percent.
